newsitem.title: USA: BASEBALL-ROBINSON BROUGHT THRILLS, RACIAL LESSONS TO BROOKLYN.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-ROBINSON BROUGHT THRILLS, RACIAL LESSONS TO BROOKLYN.

text.p: "A life is not important except in the impact it has on other lives," Jackie Robinson said.

New York City bar manager and former minor league baseball player Brian Johnston is just one of the millions of people whose lives were changed by the Brooklyn Dodger who broke the major league colour line 50 years ago.

Johnston, a native Brooklynite of Irish descent, recalls the thrills Robinson brought to Ebbets Field: "The whole place just stood up as he started to jitterbug off the first-base line. The anticipation of a steal, there would just be a roar. It was the most electric thing I had ever witnessed.

"He was so dramatic -- everything he did, the way he ran. I can picture him from the rear running down to second base, pigeon-toed. He almost wobbled. He seemed to churn up the field the way a swimmer would churn up water," he said.

"I was six in 1946 and growing up in Brooklyn, and the Dodgers were like a second religion in my home. My father and older brother were diehard Dodger fans and they (the team) were always on the radio from my earliest recollection."
But on his first trip to Ebbets Field, in 1946 when Robinson was in the minor leagues, "I committed the cardinal sin of liking the Cardinals," Johnston said.
"Then all that winter there was talk about a black man coming to the Dodgers.

"I grew up in a very, very segregated section of Brooklyn, Bay Ridge. I don't recall ever seeing a black person. The only black athlete that I had heard of at that time was Jesse Owens, and he was a national hero from the Olympics.
"And I couldn't understand why all the to-do about a black man, or a 'Negro' at that time, playing for the Dodgers."
Mastermind of the "Great Experiment" was Dodgers general manager Branch Rickey -- who previously had run the Cardinals.
"I can recall my father saying, referring to Branch Rickey, 'Why didn't he do it when he had your team?' -- referring to the Cardinals. 'Why didn't he try it then? He's going to mess up the Dodgers.'
"Waiting for that spring, there was talk about teams striking, ball players not going on the field with him, and at six years old I couldn't make out what the hell was going on.
"It just made it more dramatic. The whole neighbourhood was on pins and needles as the first game approached.
"There was talk of the Cardinals striking and some other teams, and I was very embarrassed by that. Why was my team, the world champions, why are they having a problem with this one man?"
Once Robinson started playing, Johnston said, "His cockiness bothered my father. My father would say, 'Look at the way he struts, crossing the plate in front of the catcher.'"

Eventually, said Johnston, his father came around to like Robinson. "But still if Robinson would screw up with an error or something, he'd revert back: 'What's he doing, what's he doing?' It was always like Robinson could never make a mistake.
"And most of the time he didn't -- which I think annoyed my father," Johnston said with a laugh.
But overall, Johnston said, the experience softened his father's racial attitudes: "I definitely think it changed him, and it definitely changed for me."

Thousands of people who would never show their faces in Johnston's Irish-German neighbourhood were thronging Ebbets Field: "It was filled up with black and white, it brought out the black population. It was a good lesson for me, because it struck me that we're all baseball fans."
Despite his Cardinal leanings, Johnston loved Robinson.

"He was one of my favourite players, yeah. He was always my favourite Dodger." Johnston always hit with a Jackie Robinson model bat. "One of the advantages was it had a very thick handle, you could choke up on it and still have a lot of bat."

Johnston played shortstop in the Cardinals' minor league system, coming up behind future major leaguer -- and later general manager -- Dal Maxvill, and when he had hard times he would remind himself: "JR."
"Even today when things are going rough I would remember what he went through. We didn't know what he was going through, actually, at the time. That came out later....
"But then when I found out what he went through, what people were calling him, the trouble he had, he couldn't stay at certain hotels -- I couldn't believe it."

Robinson changed racial attitudes among whites, Johnson said, as they learned of the abuse he took. "Branch Rickey picked him for that specific purpose because he knew he had fortitude and courage to withstand all that.

"But then years later, Robinson didn't take it, he got into spats and all. He wouldn't take anything from anybody. But those first couple of years he did. And it was going against really his character. He was doing it not for himself but for his whole race to get into baseball."
